rows.statement: btrfs keeps five per-device error counters: write_io_errs (failed writes), read_io_errs (failed reads), flush_io_errs (failed FLUSH writes), corruption_errs (checksum mismatch or corrupted metadata header) and generation_errs (block generation mismatch). The sysfs file devinfo/<devid>/error_stats prints the same five counters, read by the same kernel function, under shorter names (write_errs, read_errs, flush_errs, corruption_errs, generation_errs); `btrfs device stats` reads them through an ioctl.
rows.host_reading: One device (devid 1, /dev/mapper/root). All five counters are 0 in sysfs (capture lines 40-44) and through the ioctl (lines 112-116).
rows.action: None. Read the counters with `cat /sys/fs/btrfs/<fsid>/devinfo/<devid>/error_stats` (no privilege needed) or `btrfs device stats <mountpoint>`; never add -z, which zeroes them and destroys the history.

rows.statement: The counters are a persistent cumulative record: the kernel loads them from the device tree at mount, writes changes back at transaction commit, and clears them only on an explicit reset (`btrfs device stats -z`), which it logs. A non-zero counter therefore says errors happened at some time, not when. The kernel prints the same `bdev ... errs: wr ..., rd ..., flush ..., corrupt ..., gen ...` text twice: at error level when an error is counted (rate limited) and at info level at mount when any counter is non-zero. Only the error-level line dates an incident.
rows.host_reading: Counters are 0, so no mount-time line is printed; 0 `errs: wr` lines and 0 BTRFS error, critical, warning or forced-readonly lines over 6 retained boots (capture lines 154-161). Persistence across mounts cannot be observed on all-zero counters; it rests on the source.
rows.action: When a counter is non-zero, search the kernel journal of every retained boot for error-level `errs:` lines to date the errors; treat an info-level mount-time line as the stored total, not a new incident. Resetting counters stays an operator decision.

rows.statement: Scrub reads all data and metadata and checks checksums; it repairs a bad block only by copying a verified good copy from another replica. With the data profile `single` there is one copy, so a data checksum error is detected and reported as uncorrectable, not repaired. Metadata with `dup` has two logical copies on the same device and can be repaired from the second, but an SSD may store both as one physical copy. File data with the NOCOW attribute has no checksums and scrub does not verify it; systemd sets that attribute on journal files by default.
rows.host_reading: Data profile single (capture line 64); metadata and system profiles dup (`btrfs filesystem df` and sysfs allocation directories); one NVMe SSD under LUKS.
rows.action: Read this as limited self-repair, not a fault: a data checksum error on this host can be found but not fixed from a replica, so backups are the repair path for file data. Changing the data profile is an operator decision and is not proposed here.

rows.statement: No scrub record exists on this host for the root filesystem: `btrfs scrub status /` reports no stats, and /var/lib/btrfs, where btrfs-progs keeps scrub.status.<UUID> files, does not exist. The packaged monthly btrfs-scrub@.timer exists but its instance for `/` is disabled and inactive. Ordinary reads do verify checksums, so data that was read has been checked, but no record shows a full pass over stored data.
rows.host_reading: `no stats available` (capture line 121); `/var/lib/btrfs` absent (line 127); `btrfs-scrub@-.timer` disabled (line 131) and inactive (line 134). The `Error summary: no errors found` line printed beside `no stats available` is not a health reading.
rows.action: Operator decision: run `btrfs scrub start /` once or enable `btrfs-scrub@-.timer`; the lane never starts a scrub or enables a timer. After a scrub, read `btrfs scrub status /` for csum, verify, read and super errors and the corrected versus uncorrectable split.

rows.statement: smartctl 7.5 derives the NVMe overall-health line from one byte: it prints PASSED when the controller's Critical Warning byte is zero and FAILED! otherwise, and then lists the set warning bits (bit 0x01 means available spare has fallen below its threshold). Available Spare, Percentage Used and Media and Data Integrity Errors are printed but are not inputs to the PASSED or FAILED result.
rows.host_reading: PASSED with Critical Warning 0x00 (capture lines 181, 184); Available Spare 100% against threshold 10%, Percentage Used 2%, Media and Data Integrity Errors 0 (lines 186-188, 197).
rows.action: Read the Critical Warning byte and the other fields separately: a PASSED result does not mean wear or media errors were judged. Watch Percentage Used, spare against threshold and media errors as their own signals with `sudo smartctl -H -A <device>` (read-only; never -t, -s or -X).

rows.statement: The NVMe SMART / Health log reports information over the life of the controller, retained across power cycles. Power Cycles, Unexpected Power Losses (the field smartctl and nvme-cli still label Unsafe Shutdowns), Media and Data Integrity Errors and Number of Error Information Log Entries are lifetime counts, not dated events. Unexpected Power Losses increments only when main power is lost while the controller had not reported it was ready to power off, so it is not a count of host-visible crashes.
rows.host_reading: Power Cycles 325, Unsafe Shutdowns 200, Media and Data Integrity Errors 0, Error Information Log Entries 0 (capture lines 194, 196-198; nvme-cli agrees at lines 221, 223-225). Only six boots are retained in the journal, so most of the 200 cannot be dated.
rows.action: Compare two dated reads to see whether the count grew in a window; correlate growth with the journal's boot list before naming a cause. A high lifetime ratio alone is not a fault; report it to the operator as context.
